slides.0.title: Geography and climate
slides.0.subtitle: The Andes, altitude, desert irrigation and the Zonda wind
slides.1.title: A desert in the rain shadow
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Very little rain
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Most regions rarely exceed 250 mm of rain a year; San Juan averages about 150 mm
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Snowmelt irrigation
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Vineyards depend on Andean snowmelt carried by rivers such as the Mendoza, Tunuyán, San Juan and Atuel; some also use boreholes 60–200 m deep
slides.1.highlights.2.title: How irrigation has changed
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Flood irrigation was historically dominant, then furrow irrigation; drip became popular in the late 1990s
slides.1.content: No snowmelt, no vineyards: Argentina is irrigated desert viticulture.
slides.2.title: Altitude is terroir
slides.2.highlights.0.title: The altitude range
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Vineyards range from about 250 m to 3,111 m (Wine With Seth); the highest, Finca Moya in Jujuy, reaches 3,329 m. Mendoza's vineyards average about 600–1,100 m, while most European vineyards are rarely above 900 m
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Temperature and day-night swing
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Mean temperature drops roughly 0.6°C per 100 m; the day-night swing during ripening is 16–20°C, and above 20°C in many vineyards, helping to keep acidity
slides.2.highlights.2.title: UV and skins
slides.2.highlights.2.content: UV is more intense at altitude, prompting thicker skins with more anthocyanins and polyphenols
slides.2.content: In Argentina altitude adjusts temperature, light and ripening rhythm at once, so one variety changes style with elevation.
slides.3.title: Altitudes in Mendoza and the north
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Luján de Cuyo and Maipú
slides.3.highlights.0.content: The traditional heartland, with vineyards at about 800–1,100 m (Wine With Seth); another source puts Luján de Cuyo and the Uco Valley at about 850–1,520 m
slides.3.highlights.1.title: The Uco Valley
slides.3.highlights.1.content: About 900–1,400 m, cooler than central Mendoza, with more acidity and structure
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Cafayate in the north
slides.3.highlights.2.content: The town is at about 1,683 m and vineyards run from about 1,600 to over 2,000 m; Colomé's Altura Máxima in Salta reaches 3,111 m
slides.3.content: The further north, the higher the vineyards: altitude offsets the warmth of the lower latitude.
slides.4.title: The Zonda wind and other hazards
slides.4.highlights.0.title: The Zonda wind
slides.4.highlights.0.content: A hot, dry, hurricane-force wind from the Andes; if it blows at early-summer flowering it can cut yields
slides.4.highlights.1.title: Hail and frost
slides.4.highlights.1.content: Hail and frost are common hazards, covered in depth in Level 3
slides.4.highlights.2.title: Low disease pressure
slides.4.highlights.2.content: The dry climate keeps fungal disease pressure low, which suits organic viticulture
slides.4.content: The Zonda is the key word for understanding flowering-time risk in Argentina.
